Having magical powers makes you less than human, a resource to be exploited. Half-unicorn Gary Cobalt is sick of slavery, captivity, and his horn being ground down to power faster-than-light travel. When he's finally free, all he wants is to run away in his ancestors' stone ship. Instead, Captain Jenny Perata steals the ship out from under him, so she can make an urgent delivery. But Jenny held him captive for a decade, and then Gary murdered her best friend ... who was also the wife of her co-pilot, Cowboy Jim. What could possibly go right?

description: Minnesota, 1932. The Lincoln School is a pitiless place where hundreds of Native American children, forcibly separated from their parents, are sent to be educated. It is also home to an orphan named Odie O'Banion, a lively boy whose exploits earn him the superintendent's wrath. After commiting a terrible crime, Odie and his brother Albert are forced to flee, along with their best friend Mose and a brokenhearted little girl named Emmy. Together they steal away in a canoe, heading for the mighty Mississippi in search of a place to call home. Over the course of one unforgettable summer, these four orphans journey into the unknown, crossing paths with others who are adrift, from struggling farmers and traveling faith healers to displaced families and lost souls of all kinds.

description: The subject was born into a very poor trepa family in Lhoka as an illegitimate child. In this interview, he discusses being sent at the age of seven by his mother to Gongkar Chöde Monastery to become a monk. He discusses how he ran away from the monaster repeatedly and was frequently beaten by his teacher. After he finally left for good at age 15, he worked as a donkey herder and muleteer from the age of 16 to 25. He talks about his interesting experiences with receiving tax exemptions from his mother's lord [for her] by working for them, even though be belonged to a different lord via his father, and he also briefly discusses the period after 1959. [NOTE: ID numbers instead of subject names are used in OR interviews to maintain confidentiality.]

contents: Part 1. The subject was born into a very poor trepa family in Lhoka as an illegitimate child. In this interview, he discusses being sent at the age of seven by his mother to Gongkar Chöde Monastery to become a monk. He discusses how he ran away from the monaster repeatedly and was frequently beaten by his teacher. After he finally left for good at age 15, he worked as a donkey herder and muleteer from the age of 16 to 25. He talks about his interesting experiences with receiving tax exemptions from his mother's lord [for her] by working for them, even though be belonged to a different lord via his father, and he also briefly discusses the period after 1959. [NOTE: ID numbers instead of subject names are used in OR interviews to maintain confidentiality.]

Part 2. The subject was born into a very poor trepa family in Lhoka as an illegitimate child. In this interview, he tells about working as a donkey herder transporting firewood for the rukhag after he was demoted from the director's position. He was also the Deputy Xian Zhang in charge of Tsapanang Xiang, Chushul's Phu Xiang and Chushul Xiang at the time of the democratic reforms. He discusses in detail how he planted the leftover fields that used to belong to the dzong and didn't sell the grain to the State, instead using it to buy plowing animals for the masses. This action and others acts ultimately led to him being accused of stealing and embezzling from the State. Additionally, he discusses the struggles between the Gyenlo and Nyamdre revolutionary factions during the Cultural Revolution, and how the people held struggle sessions against the people in power. [NOTE: ID numbers instead of subject names are used in OR interviews to maintain confidentiality.].

description: Within this interview this individual provides details on how he first entered the monastery, at what age, and the circumstances surrounding his family when he joined. He discusses his gegen, including how he lived with him and his gegen_s livelihood. He discusses his feelings about entering the monastery, and details his education when he first arrived. He describes the living arrangements of his segment of the monastery. He discusses the nature of the shag in relation to the larger shagtsang. He then provides details on the position of the jiso, including the roles and responsibilities. He then provides details of his daily activities, including what work he did as a Gomang monk, as well as what he did for work until he ran away at age 17. Within details of the daily activities within the monastery, he describes the process of making tea with butter, the preparation of thukpa, the monks involved, and the distribution of income within the monastery.

contents: Part 1. Within this interview this individual provides details on how he first entered the monastery, at what age, and the circumstances surrounding his family when he joined. He discusses his gegen, including how he lived with him and his gegen_s livelihood.  He discusses his feelings about entering the monastery, and details his education when he first arrived.  He describes the living arrangements of his segment of the monastery.  He discusses the nature of the shag in relation to the larger shagtsang.  He then provides details on the position of the jiso, including the roles and responsibilities.  He then provides details of his daily activities, including what work he did as a Gomang monk, as well as what he did for work until he ran away at age 17.  Within details of the daily activities within the monastery, he describes the process of making tea with butter, the preparation of thukpa, the monks involved, and the distribution of income within the monastery.

Part 2. This brief interview provides a discussion of his teacher going for büdü, and how, when monks are away to Amdo, what obligations they have to their monastery.  The majority of this interview is given to details of the Gomang dispute, which was primarily based on a salary dispute among monks, and split within two factions, the pechawa and lagyüba.  This individual provides great detail on the aspects of this dispute, and how the government had to intervene within this process to settle the matter.

Part 3.This interview begins with details of how the dispute between the pechawa and lagyüba was settled by the Yigtsang and how there was no punishment of individuals.There are details of this individuals'career within the monastery, and he provides a narrative on why he ran away from the monastery, and how this issues involved his relationship with a new gegen after his previous gegen died.  He discusses how this involved two gegens actually. He also discusses how he had planned on going to India, and how this did not come about, as he became attached to the Phara Jiso, and eventually became a servant in the kitchen at Pena Gadong [tib. pa snam dga' gdong] for one year rather than continue his travels.  After the one year, he went to dö which included 6 estates and how, as a personal servant he worked mostly in the winter addressing issues of grain collection.  He provides accounts of the responsibilities of the Phara Jiso as well as the Tsangja's main work on the estates, including how his jinda was a Thangar [tib. thang dkar] Shiga, and this individual's relationship with the Phara Jiso.  He provides details on the hierarchy of who settles disputes, i.e. the Tsangja to to the 2 Jiso.  He also discusses specifics on the problems with accounts at the end of the term for Jiso.  He also provides details of the disputes between the nomads and the Jiso regarding taxes on livestock and how these disputes were settled in the past. He also provides details of the handing over , which is the accounting during the appointment of a new Jiso. He finally provides details of when he was a nyerba, a type of steward within the monastery, and responsibilities and duties of this work.

Part 4. Within this interview are descriptions of the events surrounding grain collection, and the 3 days of activities incorporated into this collection.  There are details on how the grain is examined for quality, the size of the storage facilities for the grain, and how it is sold, and the taxes surrounding this sale.  There are also descriptions of how the labor is divided up among the seasons, and how seasonal labor is hired, and what the duties of these seasonal workers are.  There are also discussions on the mibo, and the relationship of the Jiso and chandzö to the mibo.  Finally, there are details on the Dalai Lama's decree on run-away serfs, and how it was decided that after three years lords would not have hold over run-away serfs if they surrendered to the dewashung.

Part 5. This interview discusses differences between the shungdzin and bawma estates, and the miser's responsibilities on the shungdzin estate.  Details on how grain was sold and to who is also provided within this interviews, including details of how grain was exchanged for money.  This individuals also recounts several Jiso proverbs.  He discusses some history of the Drepung monastery, detailing how the 5th Dalai Lama provided authority to this monastery over particular matters.  The later half of this interviews details how disputes were settled within this individual's particular monastery, and the rights of settling disputes on the estates of the monastery, and the roles of the shidü and Jiso within this process.  Settling of individuals' disputes based on their positions (e.g. miser's lords) is also discussed.  Finally, this individuals details a specific case of dispute settlement within the monastery when an individual was killed, and how this conflict was resolved, including the positions involved.

Part 6. This interview begins with a general discussion of the position of Jiso, how this individual runs the estate, and how nyertsang has to be done prior to being eligible for the Jiso position.  This individual discusses his duties as simpön of the Tsangja and doing work for the kungö, the types of food he ate, and customs of preparing food in the monastery at this time.  Within this interview he also discusses the regulations of monks making fire for warmth.  He also provides details on how an individual, Kapshöba, purchased an estate from the monastery, the details of the transaction, the role of the government in this purchase, and monks_ reactions to this purchasing.  Finally, he provides details of how a particular Phara Jiso_s shatsang was divided.  He provides details of how a family became associated with a particular shagtsang, and how this shagtsang was eventually two branches, but same family, and divided into lay section, monk sections.  He discusses details of his own work for the lay family.  He discusses the events leading up to the family's son eventually becoming Phara Jiso in the monastery.  Finally, he discusses details of Phara Jiso's shag buying Samding [tib. bsam lding] House in Lhasa.

Part 7. This interview provides details of the position of shengo. It is discussed how the shengo provides a ceremony at least onece during his term, the appointments that the shengo makes within the monastery. This individual recounts how he was appointed to position of the Jija [tib. spyi phyag], and within this discussion he provides details of how this position is transferred, for example, how the accounting of the estates is part of this transition from old to new Jija.  He also provides details on how the Jija was appointed and how this was done through divination.  He provides details of his work as a Jija, how he had reservations about doing this work, and how he was encouraged to do this work.  He provides details of the work he did, in particular the summer, and where he was living at the time. He also provides descriptions of the position of nangsen, how this is selected, appointed, and how it is paid.  He also discusses the position of Jiso, how this individuals travels with others.  He discusses details and regulations of the jikhang [tib. spyi khang] in the monastery, and how lay persons live in these quarters.  Finally, he discusses daily work within the jikhang including details of the Chapel of the Wealth Deity called Namsekhang [tib. rnam sras khang] which was also a store room and details of the Jija and where they live.

Part 8. This interview discusses how grain is stored and how it is measured and the composition and make-up of the buildings within the monastery (e.g. which ones are for grain), including the upper Jiso (tib. simteng [gzim steng]) and the lower Jiso (tib. simshö [gzim shod]).  Also discussed  are the issues of nambu, the storage and use, how it is woven, and the materials that are used in its creation.  There are also details of the responsibilities of the Jija [tib. spyi phyag] on a daily basis, the accounting that is done daily.  There are details provided on the exchange of paper notes and coins within financial transactions with businessmen, and how the coins are distributed to the monks. The responsibilities of the Jiso are discussed, including a list of the most difficult and most common responsibilities.  There are explanations of the ordering of mangja and the relationship between this event and the endowments (tib. thebtsa [thebs rtsa], and mangja.  There are details provided on the provision of mangja from the interest accumulated on 30 dotse, and how this accounting works when distributing it to the monks.  There are details of serving tea in Mönlam, and the roles and responsibilities of the position of the tea servers, Olo in this ceremony.  There ae also details of how mangja is done in Drepung and the chabril_s relationship to the mangja.  There are details provided on how the jama work was given out as bawma to Gugi [tib. gu ge] Khamtsen monks and the income of the jama.  There are details of holding the post of Loseling nyertsang and the sources of income for this post.  There are details of the position of the chief caretaker,(tib. konyerbön [dkon gnyer dpon])and the provision of donggo with thukpa to college monks and the reasons why older monks will not partake in this thukpa. Finally, this individual provides details of when he was attempting to resign from the Phara Jiso household.

Part 9. This interview provides details on the duties involved in doing mangja, especially in relation to the position of the chama.  There is a long discussion on the collection of firewood, how a new procedure was in place to acquire firewood, and the economic issues surrounding this new procedure.  There are also details on how it was collected and the individuals generally involved in this collection.  There are also discussions on how the Simsho got the firewood, and how individuals worked with a miser in the area to get wood.  There are details on transportation of the firewood, and how it was transported to Lhasa; a road was made and how donkeys were used for transportation.  The salary of these workers is discussed.  There are details on preparation of langma, or sod, as who cut it and how it was worked.  There are also details on the shares of this for the Para Chiso.  There are also details of when this individual held position of Samdon Shig and what work he did, which was measuring the harvest grain.  He discusses how he worked with farmers, what his yields were like, and the process of replacing a work leader (leybon).  He also discusses exceptions for workers, and how these workers took days off, and where the 29 nagsen came from.

Part 10. This interview describes the Samdong Shiga, including the number of people involved on a daily basis.  There is a long discussion regarding how taxes collection is determined when a son leaves a father_s home.  There is also a long description on the details of a specific loan collection, part of the Loseling loan collecting, and how this individual made loans, and details of consultations with the Shido at this time.  There are also issues discussed surrounding the planting of the fields, and the accounting of these.  There is a story of a cripple who worked the lands, and how, when the time came, his lands were divided up.  There are then details of what happens when a person has tax responsibilities, such as when land is inherited.  These issues are directly related to when a son separates from his home, and the monastery_s lack of role in this issue.  There is also a description of when and under what circumstances the Shido is involved in disputes between father and son.  There is also a brief description of the punishment authority of the Chiso.  There are also discussions of the Shido_s role in repossessing a deceased person_s property.  There are also details provided of the salary for workers hired by the Shidu and the nomad miser taxes, and when the mibo payment is collected, and the responsibilities of nyerba in a mitsen.

Part 11. This interview describes the difference between mitsen chondze and tratsang chondze and the Enchondze - what this position is and what it includes.  The differences beween getting gye outside in inside the dukhang are also described.  There is also a description of who hands out phog in Gomang, either the Chabu or the servant, and the custom of monks in bringing out phog and the accounting of gye, and how these items are accounted for within the monastery.  There are also descriptions of how monks differentiate between different types of gye.  There are descriptions of the relationship between Khamtsen and Mitsen, who you ask to be a khamtsen mitsen.  There is also details of the hiring process of monks and lay persons to collect firewood and the issues surrounding this task.  There is also a description of a book with particular procedures written in it that is followed by monks for certain activities.  There is finally a detailed description of the making of khabse, the individuals involved within this process and how long it takes.

Part 12. This interview discusses his responsibilities as a jija within the monastery, and how he dealt with other monks stealing.  He discusses also the various ways in which he made money and how he associated these money-making activities with the fact that he was no longer celibate.  He discusses how much he made in planting fields and various financial arrangements he made with a family in order to lend out grain.  He discusses how he wanted to be released from the monastery due to his non-celibate status, but the monastery kept him on, as they needed him to work and discusses the responsibilities he had at this time.  He also remembers how the Chinese came and wanted him to sell them dru and the agreements that had to make in order to do this.  He also discusses a specific incident of collecting on a loan and taking the individual's guns in lieu of money, and how this caused problems with the Chinese.

Part 13. This interview provides a listing of all of the monastery_s estates, who held these estates (e.g. Chiso or monastery), and how these were ranked in terms of sonkhal.  There are descriptions of the Donggo of Chiso, including details of the serving of food and tea at various times, the amounts served, and to whom.  For example, there are descriptions of the barum and tea for monks, and how the barum was prepared, and the regulations surrounding tea distribution.  There are details on where the wheat is ground into flour and the process for this and the time it takes.  There are also descriptions of the Chiso phog, and how the Chomon is provided during the 12th Tibetan month, who does the work for Laji, and what the Chsio nangnyer do.  There is also an account of an individuals who ran away and of his tongba lands.  There is also an explanation of the Zhu Rten, a gift provided to lenders.  Finally, the interview concludes with a description of what monks were thinking about in the late 50_s and their perspectives on the Chinese.

Part 14. In this brief interview, this individual describes the nature of the Chushigandru's requests for help from the monastery and what he thought about this group fighting the Chinese. He also discusses briefly the payment of barley to the monks, and he discusses the changes he would have made in Drepun monastery.

Part 15. Within this interview, this individual discusses details of his family and how he first became a monk, and the details of the ceremony with the monastery_s abbot in order to become a student.  He provides details on the processes of studying and taking exams.  He makes distinctions between gyu tre and gyudro chemo.  He discusses the livelihood of his teacher and himself, and how they lived.  He discusses in details the various positions he held in the monastery, their names, and the responsibilities he had.  He discusses, for example, doing mitsen chontse and the lack of funds with this position.  He also discusses merging within a larger shagtsang after his teacher died, the conflicts there, and why he ran away.  He also discusses how he got rabjung, and provides details on the teaching of children within the monastery.  He finally discusses the various positions within the monastery that one must do, and the steps included in this process.  He also discusses issues about poor families_ seeking a teacher, and the issues surrounding this process.

Part 16. The interview provides significant biographical detail of this individual, including his perceptions of which life is better, that of the nomad layperson, of the household, or that of a monk, and why he believes this.  He discusses in detail how he was able to get out of his responsibilities as a monk, and what he would do with his time when he was avoiding studying.  He also discusses issues surrounding visiting his family.  The later half of the interview contains a lengthy detailed narrative on how he was able to get out of being the servant to a lord named Ser Laji as well as some detail on his family life after he was not a monk.  He also discusses issues surrounding older monks and the taking of tsamba.

notes: Recording of visit with Mrs. Mary Newsome at the Colony Home, a nursing facility for the elderly, Fitzgerald GA: Mary Newsome sings, then others in the room (including nursing home staff) coax her to sing more, male voice is staff member Daniel Purdom, Mary Newsome sings, Daniel Purdom asks Mary to sing the "Promised Land," Mary Newsome sings "Promised Land" as others around Mary join in, repeat of the song sung by Mary Newsome alone, Newsome talks about church sings in the past, Mary Newsome begins another song but stops in the middle, musical therapist Nan Lee asks Mary to begin a song, group sings "Jacob's Ladder," Mary Newsome sings "Steal Away," Claudia Golden, another resident at the home, finishes the song "Steal Away," Daniel Purdom asks Mary about her ideas about Heaven is like, and about the Bible, group encourages Mary to sing "Long White Robe," Nan Lee asks Mary Newsome about her father, Mary Newsome sings "Steal Away" joined by Nan Lee, Daniel Purdom asks about her past and Mary Newsome talks about the cotton picking days, says that her brother was named Willie, Mary was her mother's name, does not remember her father's name; additional conversation; Mary Newsome sings "I'm Almost Home" (repeats), Claudia Golden adds to the song, additional conversation, Purdom asks Mary about the "Long White Robe," Mary Newsome sings a different song.

Fieldworker Beverly Robinson's notes report that Mrs. Mary Newsome was born on March 11, 1872, and, in 1977, she lived at the Colony [Nursing] Home. The name is spelled Mary Newsom in a 1979 Georgia death certificate. Robinson's notes indicate that Newsome had been described as having some recall of work songs, "field songs which led me to her"; Robinson also quotes a nursing home worker as stating, "Mrs. Newsome is restricted to a wheelchair and has suffered partial hearing loss, her memory span has decreased within the last few years and she is disoriented at times." Project documentation indicates that Robinson visited Mrs. Newsome three times and made sound recordings identified by call numbers AFC 1982/010: AFS 21110 (11 July 1977), AFC 1982/010: AFS 21118 (4 August 1977), AFS 21119 and AFS 21120 (between 4 and 11 August 1977), and call number AFC 1982/010: AFS 21080 (August 11, 1977); Robinson also copied the pre-existing recording of Mrs. Newsome's singing presented at call number AFC 1982/010: AFS 21070.

notes: Recordings of examples of religious music collected during the South-Central Georgia Folklife Project selected by the folklorist Dennis Coelho: "Home Bells Are Ringing" recorded at the Ben Hill County Singing Convention, Fitzgerald GA, sung by all attendees, accompanied by piano; "I am a stranger here below" performed by the congregation of Mt. Paran Primitive Baptist Church, Berrien County GA, this selection is hymn number 380 in a recent version of Benjamin Lloyd's Primitive Hymns (full title: The Primitive Hymns, Spiritual Songs, and Sacred Poems, Regularly Selected, Classified and Set In Order, and Adapted To Social Singing and all Occasions of Divine Worship), first published 1841; "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot" and "Steal Away" recorded at an informal singing get-together at the home of Fannie Lee Teals, Tifton GA; "New Britain," called "Amazing Grace" by the song leader, number 45 in the Original Sacred Harp hymnal, recorded at the South Georgia Sacred Harp Singing Convention held in the church at Georgia Agrirama (subsequently renamed Georgia Museum of Agriculture and Historic Village), Tifton GA; "Hebron," Original Sacred Harp number 566, recorded at the same event as the preceding; "Uncloudy Day," recorded at the Bethel Baptist Church Homecoming, Worth County GA; "Inside the Pearly Gates," with the "notes" or "fa-sol-la" preceding the lyrics, and "Send it on Down," sung without the preceding "notes," at the shape note singing convention held at the Mt. Zion Missionary Baptist Church, Damascus GA.

Following project fieldwork in 1977, the sponsoring agency, the Arts Experiment Station at Abraham Baldwin Agricultural College in Tifton, Georgia, engaged Dennis Coelho as folklorist-in-residence to support community outreach and continue project research. His initial activity was to assess the field project collection and select a cross section of recordings for educators and community access. The result, completed in 1978, is a set of three recordings: secular music, spoken word and narrative, and religious music.

description: This post presents several folktales from the Bahamas focusing on the adventures of the tricky, resourceful folktale hero Jack. We’ll see Jack escaping from the giants by charming them with his musical instrument and witness his courtship with the Devil’s daughter, Greenleaf. Like most Bahamian folktales, these stories contain complex wordplay and have songs embedded in the tales. The two tales here are very distinctively part of the Jack tale tradition, which must have been brought to the Bahamas with English settlers, but they also have African and other elements springing from their complex Caribbean roots. They were recorded by Alan Lomax and Mary Elizabeth Barnicle in 1935.

description: Seminal Vermont organic farmers Jack Lazor and Anne Lazor of Butterworks Farm in Westfield, Vermont, talk about going back to the land after college; their early efforts at raising grains and beans; their shift to dairy and the development of a market for yogurt; and the importance of organic agriculture. They also discuss the generational transfer of their farm to their daughter and son-in-law.
